c.tagline: The Amazon's improbable metropolis, reachable only by river or air.

taxi.fareNote: There are no ride-hailing apps and few car taxis; the ubiquitous three-wheeled mototaxis (motocarros) are the main way to get around. Agree the fare before setting off — most rides within the city are only a few soles.

emergency.note: Dial 105 for the National Police and 116 for the SAMU ambulance service; 116 also covers medical emergencies nationwide.

hood_landmark.Belén: Belen market floating city Iquitos Peru
hood_landmark.Centro (Plaza de Armas): Plaza de Armas Iquitos Casa de Fierro
hood_landmark.San Juan Bautista: Mercado de Artesania San Juan Iquitos

avoid.reason: Caution in the Belén market area

hood_desc: The compact historic core around the Plaza de Armas, the Gothic cathedral, and the Gustave Eiffel-designed Casa de Fierro (Iron House), lined with faded rubber-boom mansions and most of the city's hotels; the natural base for first-timers.
The riverside boulevard (Malecón Tarapacá) and adjoining Boulevard, a breezy promenade of bars, restaurants, and craft stalls high above the Amazon, liveliest at sunset and after dark.

The iconic 'floating city' district by the river, home to the sprawling Belén market where jungle produce, fish, and traditional medicine are sold, and to stilt-and-raft houses that rise and fall with the river; a raw, unmissable local sight best seen by morning.

The northern port district by the Nanay River, where boats leave for jungle lodges and the Amazon proper, and locals gather at the Nanay river beach; a workaday, quieter riverside area away from the tourist core.
The southern district near the airport and the large San Juan artisan market, a spread-out, residential area and the main place to buy Amazonian handicrafts.

water.note: Drink bottled or purified water only.

transit.hours: Mototaxis run essentially around the clock; river boats and ferries follow daytime departure schedules that vary by route and river level.
transit.note: Iquitos has no metro or rail and, uniquely for a city its size, no road connection to the outside world — mototaxis and motorcycles dominate the streets, while river boats link it to the rest of the Amazon.
transit.pay: Mototaxi fares are paid in cash (soles) directly to the driver and agreed in advance; boat tickets are bought in cash at the ports of Bellavista Nanay and Puerto Masusa.

air: Coronel FAP Francisco Secada Vignetta International Airport (IQT)
bus: No intercity road links — the city is not connected to Peru's road network
ferry: River boats and cargo ferries to Nauta, Santa Rosa (for Leticia/Tabatinga), Yurimaguas, and Pucallpa along the Amazon and its tributaries

airport.name: Coronel FAP Francisco Secada Vignetta International Airport (IQT)

transit.m: Mototaxi from the airport to the Plaza de Armas (~20-30 min)
Car taxi to the city center (20-30 min)

tip.r: Not expected for mototaxis or casual meals; rounding up or leaving about 10% at nicer restaurants and for guides is appreciated.

food.name: Juane
food.desc: Turmeric rice packed with chicken, egg and olives, wrapped in bijao leaves and boiled into a fragrant green bundle.

places.name: Blanquita
places.note: Long-running local canteen famous for juanes and everyday Amazonian plates at low prices.

places.name: Huasai
places.note: Institution for regional set lunches; juane is a staple of the daily menu.

places.name: Mercado de Belen
places.note: Market cooks sell fresh-boiled juanes wrapped in leaves every morning.

food.name: Tacacho con cecina
food.desc: Roasted green plantain mashed with pork fat and served with smoked, salted pork cecina; the classic Iquitos breakfast.

places.name: Huasai
places.note: Reliable, generous version served all day alongside other jungle staples.

places.name: Blanquita
places.note: Locals queue here for the smoky cecina and chorizo regional.

places.name: Mercado Bellavista Nanay
places.note: Riverside market stalls griddle tacacho to order for boat passengers.

food.name: Paiche
food.desc: Giant Amazon river fish, firm and mild, served grilled, breaded as chicharron or raw in ceviche with charapita chilli.

places.name: Al Frio y Al Fuego
places.note: Iquitos signature floating restaurant; grilled paiche and paiche ceviche with a pool and skyline view.

places.name: Amazon Bistro
places.note: French-Amazonian bistro on the riverfront doing refined paiche plates.

places.name: Dawn on the Amazon Cafe
places.note: Traveller favourite with careful hygiene and well-priced fish dishes.

food.name: Patarashca
food.desc: River fish seasoned with sacha culantro, tomato and charapita, wrapped in bijao leaves and cooked over coals until steamy.

places.name: Al Frio y Al Fuego
places.note: Wood-fire kitchen turns out one of the city's best patarashcas.

places.name: Huasai
places.note: Everyday regional menu that reliably includes patarashca and inchicapi.

places.name: Fitzcarraldo Restaurant Bar
places.note: Corner terrace institution serving Amazonian classics to riverfront tables.

food.name: Inchicapi de gallina
food.desc: Thick hen soup blended with peanuts, corn flour and sacha culantro; the comfort dish of the Loreto jungle.

places.name: Blanquita
places.note: Home-style version at menu-del-dia prices, popular with office workers.

places.name: Huasai
places.note: Regional soups rotate daily; inchicapi is the most requested.

places.name: Mercado de Belen
places.note: Market comedores ladle it out from dawn, thick and peanut-rich.

food.name: Suri (palm weevil grubs)
food.desc: Fat aguaje-palm grubs skewered and grilled or fried; buttery and nutty, a genuine Amazon street delicacy.

places.name: Mercado de Belen
places.note: The classic place to try suri, grilled to order on charcoal at the stalls.

places.name: Mercado Bellavista Nanay
places.note: Smaller, calmer market where vendors skewer suri fresh each morning.

places.name: Al Frio y Al Fuego
places.note: Serves a cleaner, restaurant-style suri starter if the market feels daunting.

food.name: Camu camu juice
food.desc: Tart pink juice from an Amazon river fruit with famously huge vitamin C levels; served ice cold and lightly sweetened.

places.name: Dawn on the Amazon Cafe
places.note: Fresh juices made with filtered water, a favourite for camu camu and aguaje.

places.name: Mercado de Belen
places.note: Juice stalls blend camu camu, cocona and aguaje to order for a few soles.

places.name: Karma Cafe
places.note: Relaxed riverfront cafe with jungle-fruit juices and smoothies.

food.name: Chuchuhuasi macerado
food.desc: Amazonian bark steeped in cane spirit with honey; the best known of the jungle tonics known locally as siete raices.

places.name: Pasaje Paquito, Mercado de Belen
places.note: Legendary alley of stalls selling every jungle macerado, chuchuhuasi included.

places.name: La Noche
places.note: Popular riverfront bar pouring macerados and cocktails late into the night.

places.name: Fitzcarraldo Restaurant Bar
places.note: Sit-down spot to sample macerados with food rather than at a market stall.

landmarks: Belén Market and floating district
An exuberant riverside market of jungle produce, medicinal barks and stilt-and-raft houses, the raw, unforgettable soul of Amazonian Iquitos.
Casa de Fierro (Iron House)
A rubber-boom curiosity attributed to Gustave Eiffel's workshops, its bolted iron panels shipped from Europe and reassembled on the Plaza de Armas.
Malecón Tarapacá
Iquitos's riverfront promenade of rubber-era mansions and azulejo tiles, where the whole city gathers for sunsets over the Itaya River.
Plaza de Armas de Iquitos
The city's palm-lined main square, framed by the neo-Gothic Iglesia Matriz and the faded glories of rubber-boom architecture.
Iglesia Matriz de Iquitos (San Juan Bautista)
A striking early-20th-century church whose Gothic-style spire and Swiss clock tower preside over the Plaza de Armas.
Amazon Rescue Center (CREA)
A heartwarming sanctuary rehabilitating orphaned Amazonian manatees, where visitors meet these gentle giants before their return to the wild.
Pilpintuwasi Butterfly Farm and Amazon Animal Orphanage
A riverboat-reached refuge at Padre Cocha breeding iridescent butterflies and sheltering rescued jaguars, monkeys and macaws.
Quistococha Lagoon and Tourist Park
A jungle lagoon with an artificial beach, zoo and paiche fish tanks, the locals' favorite weekend escape outside the city.
Pacaya-Samiria National Reserve
Peru's largest protected flooded forest, the 'jungle of mirrors,' where multi-day boat expeditions from Iquitos reveal pink dolphins and macaws.
Allpahuayo-Mishana National Reserve
A biodiversity hotspot on white-sand forest just outside Iquitos, famed among birders for species found nowhere else on Earth.

train.note: There is no railway anywhere in the Peruvian Amazon. Iquitos is the largest city in the world with no road connection to the outside - you arrive by river or by air, and Peru has no international passenger trains in any case.

bus.note: There are no intercity coaches because there are no roads out of Iquitos. The one highway runs 100 km south to Nauta, served by shared vans and colectivos from the Túpac Amaru terminal. Within the city, moto-taxis are the universal transport.

intl.to: Santa Rosa, for Leticia in Colombia and Tabatinga in Brazil (Peru) - fast boat ~10-12 hr, slow boat ~2-3 days
intl.op: Transtur / Golfinho fast-boat operators — tickets at the Iquitos riverfront agencies

intl.to: Pucallpa & Yurimaguas (Peru) - slow cargo-passenger boats, 3-5 days
intl.op: Eduardo / Henry riverboat lines — tickets at Puerto Masusa

ferry.note: The Amazon is the only surface route out. Fast boats downriver to Santa Rosa on the Peru-Colombia-Brazil frontier take a long day and leave early in the morning; slow boats take two to three days with a hammock on deck. Get your Peruvian exit stamp before boarding, as immigration is not handled onboard. Upriver services to Pucallpa and Yurimaguas connect to Peru's road network and take three to five days. Departures slip constantly - treat schedules as approximate.

half.name: Monkey Island (Isla de los Monos)
half.blurb: A river-island primate rescue reserve reached by boat along the Amazon and Itaya rivers, with free-roaming rehabilitated monkeys.

half.name: Yagua Native Community
half.blurb: An indigenous Yagua settlement reachable by boat where traditional blowgun demonstrations and thatched dwellings can be seen.

half.name: Nauta & the River Confluence
half.blurb: A river town about ninety minutes by road where the Marañón and Ucayali rivers meet to form the Amazon proper.
